Update, 2020-03-26

7,431 confirmed cases, 1,019 of them new today; 434 deaths, 78 of them new today.

Compared with the 21st, five days ago, confirmed cases have doubled and deaths have tripled. That’s almost the same doubling rate as in my update on the 21st, measured against the four days before it. At this rate, there will be 15,000 confirmed cases by the end of the month, and deaths will pass 1,000. I’ll keep watching. I hope the measures work and my prediction turns out to be nonsense.

The Dutch public health institute, RIVM, published this explanation today:


I didn’t understand the first paragraph.

How exactly can they tell the numbers are “increasing less quickly”?

Maybe like this:

Yesterday there were 341 new hospital admissions, today 315;

yesterday there were 80 deaths, today 78.

Hence the conclusion that the increase is slowing. Going back further, admissions did fall from more than a thousand to just over 300. But is that because fewer people need care, or because there aren’t enough medical resources to admit them?

Now look at the deaths: 80 yesterday, 63 the day before, 34 the day before that, and 78 today, two fewer than yesterday.

Put those two together, and they hastily conclude that the increase is slowing.

I don’t know whether RIVM never studied statistics, doesn’t follow the news from Spain, China and Italy, or thinks the public is easy to fool.

But none of that is the main point.

Don’t confirmed cases count when you decide whether the increase is slowing? 545, 811, 852, 1,019. Ha.


Look at the last sentence: they no longer report the youngest age among the dead. Before, it was someone in their fifties. Maybe a young person has died now, and they don’t want to cause panic.

I sat out on my balcony for a while. The neighbors were walking their dogs, exercising, going to the supermarket; you couldn’t tell anything was different. Things got a bit better after the prime minister stressed on Monday how important it is to stay at home.

Just not good enough.


WHO: Test, test, test!

The Netherlands:


March 21: 3,631 confirmed cases, 136 deaths, 637 new cases in a single day. Confirmed cases have doubled in four days and deaths have tripled, yet the Dutch cabinet still hasn’t taken further measures and is still waiting to see. The epidemic scared off the cabinet minister in charge of medical care, nobody wanted to clean up the mess, and so they pulled in a stand-in from an opposition party.

The government’s attitude is interesting, too. On the 16th the prime minister said in a televised address that the country would go the herd immunity route. A few days later, apparently after a poor public reaction, he quickly changed his tune: herd immunity is not the method but the result, the goal to be reached. Yesterday the king also gave a televised address to the nation and said a lot of bland, irrelevant things. Even my mom could tell: what is he even talking about?!

Germany, the Netherlands, the UK and Switzerland seem to have formed an alliance, dragging their feet on tough measures; closing schools and restaurants took ages of dithering. Today the Netherlands even said it plans to reopen restaurants and bars in three weeks. Excuse me?



The other camp in Europe, led by France, Spain and Italy, went straight for a full lockdown, and their governments were remarkably resolute, although enforcement clearly fell short. French President Macron’s televised address came right after the Dutch prime minister’s, but his stance could not have been more different: he kept stressing that this is a war (“We are at war”). The Dutch cabinet, by comparison, acted like proper politicians and gave the people three options: do nothing, total lockdown, or measured intervention.

The Netherlands chose the third option.

I went on Twitter and YouTube to see how the Dutch public reacted. Some people were against it, but slightly more were in favor. The comment I saw most was “clearly and well spoken.” Seriously, is this a speech contest? Clear diction, clear delivery, so shall we pin a big red paper flower on the prime minister and give him a Young Pioneer captain’s armband, like a model pupil?

The way European governments and citizens, from the top down, have reacted during this period has made me rethink the so-called Western system and the Western public’s capacity for independent thought.

Back when the epidemic broke out in China, around the end of January, I told my colleagues I was vaguely worried and wanted to buy masks. My Dutch colleagues looked at me as if I were an idiot, then brainwashed me with the “coronavirus trinity”: the virus is no different from ordinary flu; if it’s dangerous at all, it’s mainly to old people; and masks protect other people, not you. What could I say? I shrugged. You never know.

Before I knew it, it was late February, and on February 27 the Netherlands finally had its first case. Germany had already been showing signs of an outbreak, so the first Dutch case was only a matter of time. The really rotten luck was that it coincided with Carnival… The guy who was the first confirmed case in the Netherlands had even been to the parade in Tilburg. It’s hard to believe that North Brabant becoming the worst-hit province has nothing to do with the Carnival parades, though the government hasn’t said so outright. Intensive care beds are now in desperately short supply, and attempts to transfer critical patients elsewhere have stalled because nobody will take them.

After the first case was confirmed, I told my colleagues again at work that I was worried and that we needed masks, and again I got the trinity. Still in denial at this point; I was speechless. I can’t win this argument with you, so I’ll just look after myself. A few days later, the government spoke about how serious the epidemic was for the first time, and that hit the Dutch where it hurt. They started stockpiling, and not just a little: they bought huge piles of stuff. They’d been proven wrong, but I wasn’t going to kick them while they were down ↓↓


From then on the epidemic got worse by the day. Every day people paid closer and humbler attention to what was really happening, and yet they stayed very, very careless.

Like still gathering to chat in the office;

like the people in Germany who, with work stopped in some places and restaurants closed, chose to throw coronavirus parties on the grass in the park (Are you f**king retarded?);

like the neighbors I message with, who still think a lockdown isn’t the best option because it damages the economy and makes going to the supermarket inconvenient (?!?!);

like the colleague who threw a birthday party at home for his wife, and another colleague who brought his child, who had a cold, to the party…

like today, when I can still see family after family driving and cycling past my window, and online I saw people “on vacation” on the beach in The Hague;

like the Saturday fish market in the Netherlands, still packed with people…


Western society has always criticized the Chinese for lacking critical thinking. At a moment like this, what has happened to their thinking? Why do they keep forcing me to revise my impression of them? Why do they let the government and mainstream media lead them by the nose, then wholeheartedly and unthinkingly adopt these wrong views as their own, argue for them and believe them without a shred of doubt?

Then think of the stereotypes about China and Asia that crop up now and then in everyday conversation, connect them with the line the mainstream media take, and it starts to make sense.

But I digress.

Back to the government.


Watch the video in the original answer on Zhihu

00:15 How governments deal with an epidemic

I came across it via @Xue Wen.


I’ve watched this video dozens of times. An absolute classic.


Stage one: nothing is going to happen.

Stage two: something may be going to happen, but we should do nothing about it.

Stage three: maybe we should do something about it, but there’s nothing we can do.

Stage four: maybe there was something we could have done, but it’s too late now.


Add the politicians’ classic facial expressions, and it’s perfect.


The Dutch cabinet doesn’t want to lock down cities or the country simply because it fears that if this drags on with no end in sight, the economy will take a heavy blow. So it chose to boil the frog slowly. But they haven’t looked around at the countries that took strict measures, like China, South Korea and Singapore, with China’s measures of course the strictest. Without the resolve to strictly limit people going out and to test on a massive scale, boiling the frog slowly like this could very well end with the epidemic out of control and the economy badly hit anyway: a perfect lose-lose.

For a country as small as the Netherlands, with barely 17 million people, the epidemic is keeping pace with the big Western European countries. What an achievement. Confirmed cases have passed 3,600, but the real number is at least several times higher, because the Netherlands long ago stopped testing mild cases and patients’ family members. Add the infected people without symptoms who keep roaming around freely, and who knows what the real number is?

It’s not as if the Dutch government has done nothing. It has closed schools and restaurants, advised people to go out less and, when they do, to keep 1.5 m apart. In truth, everyone knows these recommendations are useless. People go out when they want to go out and have fun when they want to have fun, and when they’re in the mood, who’s going to measure the distance with a ruler? People are the same everywhere: without enforcement, don’t count on self-discipline to wipe out a virus.


This is the most objective and scientific article on the epidemic I’ve read (there’s a Traditional Chinese translation at the end):

https://medium.com/@tomaspueyo/coronavirus-the-hammer-and-the-dance-be9337092b56


Here’s one of its charts:


As you can see, mitigation (the red line), which is roughly what the Netherlands is doing, only slows the epidemic to a limited extent and does nothing to contain it fundamentally. The green “hammer” line stands for tough measures like those in China and South Korea: a hard blow to the virus so that it can’t rise again.

If you look only at the fatality rate of the virus, it’s actually not that bad; as some people say, it may be similar to ordinary flu. The problem is that the new coronavirus is extremely contagious, and what really drives the death rate is the number of critical patients relative to medical resources. Take the US: what would happen if it did nothing at all? In the chart below, the red line is the number of ICU beds in the US, the blue bars are hospitalizations and the dark blue bars are critical cases.


With medical resources stretched far too thin, mild cases become severe and severe cases face death.


As for the fatal flaws in herd immunity thinking: first, herd immunity is supposed to be achieved through antibodies, not through the virus, and the difference between the two needs no explanation. Second, it completely ignores mutation. OK, so you let most people get infected and develop antibodies, and sacrifice some people. Then what? The next year the virus mutates, you go for herd immunity again and sacrifice some more people. The idea must be to raise GDP per capita.

I’m not much into politics, but this epidemic really does make many things clear and gets you thinking. I believe that whatever the system, East or West, leaders put their own interests and power above the interests, and even the lives, of ordinary people. That much is beyond doubt. One side covered things up and then turned extremely tough; the other is lukewarm and keeps fleecing its own people. Judging by the results, though, the former seems to have worked better. If you keep making blunders yourself, don’t blame your rivals for cashing in. Lately I’ve had a strong feeling that Western society today looks a lot like China’s Qing dynasty under the Qianlong Emperor, its high point before the long decline.


In times like these, look after yourselves.
